abstract: A Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research policy brief that weighs the evidence on AI's labor market effects against the "AI jobs apocalypse" framing amplified by media coverage and by AI company leaders. Its central empirical contribution is an IPUMS-CPS analysis of unemployment by AI-exposure quintile: since 2022 the unemployment rate for the most-exposed quintile rose by 0.77 percentage points while the least-exposed quintile rose slightly more, by 0.85 percentage points. The brief concludes that aggregate employment effects are likely small so far, that productivity effects are positive but uneven, and that firm adoption is accelerating unevenly. It treats the weak market for new graduates as the one area where AI is a plausible partial cause, while cautioning that entry-level hiring declines are not clearly visible until 2024, which complicates attribution to ChatGPT's late-2022 launch.
keyFindings: Unemployment for the top quintile of AI-exposed workers rose 0.77 percentage points since 2022; for the least-exposed quintile it rose 0.85 percentage points. The differential implies no measurable net AI displacement in aggregate US employment.
Employment growth in coding-heavy occupations has slowed but remains positive, and online job postings for software developers have grown faster than for other occupations over the last year.
Among firms that adopted enterprise AI, employment grew by 10 percent in the two years following adoption, an effect driven by firms with the highest per capita AI spending.
In Census BTOS data, only 5 percent of firms report any employment impact from AI, with equal numbers reporting gains and losses.

New-graduate unemployment reached 5.6 percent in early 2026, up 1.6 percentage points from three years earlier. The brief notes entry-level declines are not notable until 2024, making pure AI attribution to the 2022 ChatGPT launch difficult.

Firm adoption estimates diverge sharply by instrument: Census BTOS (the most conservative, nationally representative) puts firm AI use near 20 percent, while a household survey finds over 40 percent of employed respondents use AI at work and Ramp estimates over 50 percent of its clients spend on AI tools.

Productivity results are positive but heterogeneous and concentrated among less-experienced workers: 15 percent overall in customer support with 30 percent for novices, and 56 percent faster task completion with GitHub Copilot, against a more modest 10-30 percent range in a separate software deployment study.
methodology: Policy brief synthesizing published research with original descriptive analysis of IPUMS-CPS microdata. The headline exposure result plots quarterly unemployment rates by AI-exposure quintile from 2015 to 2026, comparing the change since 2022 across the top and bottom quintiles. Supporting figures reproduce Stanford Digital Economy Lab and ADP Research employment indices by age group for customer service representatives and software developers, drawn from a five-year balanced sample of firms using ADP payroll services, indexed to 100 at the November 2022 ChatGPT launch. Firm adoption figures are taken from the Census Business Trends and Outlook Survey and compared against household surveys and private payroll and spend data.
qualifiers: This is a policy brief rather than a peer-reviewed paper, and most of the productivity and entry-level results are restatements of primary studies already tracked elsewhere in this corpus (Brynjolfsson/Chandar/Chen, Brynjolfsson/Li/Raymond, Crane and Soto). The novel contribution is the exposure-quintile unemployment comparison, which is descriptive rather than causally identified: it compares raw unemployment trends across exposure quintiles without controlling for sectoral or demographic composition, so it bounds the aggregate effect rather than estimating it. The 0.77 and 0.85 percentage-point figures are reported to two decimals but the differential between them (-0.08pp) is well within sampling noise, which is why it is plotted at zero rather than as a negative displacement estimate. The 10 percent employment growth among AI adopters is conditional on adoption and subject to selection: the brief itself notes elsewhere that adopting firms were already growing faster before adoption.
